units.t: The Fundamental Attribution Error.
Part one. The essay nobody chose.
Picture yourself in traffic.
A car swerves in front of you with barely a metre to spare, then speeds off.
What's your first thought?
For most of us, it's something short and unprintable about what kind of person that driver must be.
Now picture the last time you cut someone off.
You probably didn't think, I'm a terrible person.
You thought, I didn't see them, or I was about to miss my exit, or I was running late for something important.
That gap in how we explain the same behaviour is what this lesson is about.
When other people do something wrong, we tend to blame their character.
When we do the same thing, we tend to blame the situation.
Psychologists call the first half of this the fundamental attribution error.
It's our habit of over-explaining other people's behaviour by who they are, and under-explaining it by the circumstances they're in.
One of the earliest demonstrations came in 1967, from the American psychologists Edward Jones and Victor Harris.
They gave people short essays about Fidel Castro, the leader of Cuba.
Some essays praised Castro and some criticised him.
Readers were asked what the writer really thought of him.
Here's the clever part.
Some readers were told the writer had been free to choose which side to argue.
Others were told the writer had been assigned a side, like a debater given a topic.
You'd expect the second group to shrug and say, well, you can't tell what they believe.
They didn't.
Even when they knew the side had been assigned, readers still judged that a pro-Castro essay came from someone fairly pro-Castro.
They took the words as a window into the writer's character, even when the situation fully explained them.
A decade later, in 1977, the Stanford psychologist Lee Ross gave the effect its grand name.
He and his colleagues also ran one of its most elegant tests.
Pairs of students were randomly assigned to be either a quizmaster or a contestant.
The quizmaster made up ten hard general knowledge questions from their own areas of interest, and the contestant tried to answer them.
Of course the contestants struggled.
The questions came from the quizmaster's own pet topics.
Yet when everyone rated how knowledgeable each person was, the contestants and the observers watching rated the quizmasters as clearly smarter.
The roles had been handed out at random, and everyone knew it.
People still read the situation's advantage as a difference in brains.
Why do we do this?
One big reason is simply what fills our view.
When we watch someone else, the person is the most visible thing in the scene, while the pressures on them are hidden.
When we act ourselves, we can't see our own face, but we see every pressure around us.
In 1973, the psychologist Michael Storms tested this with video.
After a conversation, he showed people a recording shot from the other person's point of view.
Seeing themselves from the outside, people explained their own behaviour more in terms of their personality, and observers who saw things through the actor's eyes leaned more on the situation.
Change the camera angle, and the explanation changes with it.
In the next part, we'll see just how powerful situations can be, in a study involving a parable about helping strangers.
Part two. The hurried Samaritans.
In 1973, the psychologists John Darley and Daniel Batson ran a study at Princeton Theological Seminary.
The participants were students training for the ministry, people you might expect to be especially kind.
Each student was asked to prepare a short talk and then walk to another building to deliver it.
Some were asked to speak about the parable of the Good Samaritan, the story of a traveller who stops to help a stranger lying injured by the road.
Before they set off, some students were told they had plenty of time.
Others were told they were already late and needed to hurry.
On the way, each student passed a man slumped in a doorway, coughing and groaning.
He was part of the study.
The question was simple.
Who would stop?
The biggest factor wasn't personality or religious outlook.
It wasn't even the topic of the talk.
It was time.
Of the students who thought they had time to spare, about six in ten offered help.
Of the students who'd been told to hurry, only about one in ten did.
Some of the hurrying students, on their way to give a talk about the Good Samaritan, literally stepped over the man.
Now imagine you'd walked past and seen one of those students ignore someone in distress.
You'd almost certainly have judged them as cold or selfish.
You wouldn't have known they'd just been told they were late.
That's the fundamental attribution error in action.
We see the behaviour clearly, but the situation is usually invisible to us.
The effect isn't the same everywhere.
In 1994, Michael Morris and Kaiping Peng compared how an English-language American newspaper and a Chinese-language newspaper reported the same two murder cases in the United States.
The American coverage leaned more on the killers' personal traits, such as a bad temper or a mental instability.
The Chinese-language coverage leaned more on circumstances, such as relationships, pressures and social isolation.
Later research suggests people from more collectivist cultures do still make the error, but often a bit less strongly.
There's also an honest caveat.
The neat idea that we always blame others' character and our own circumstances has been questioned.
A large review in 2006 by Bertram Malle found that this mirror-image pattern is weaker and patchier than textbooks once claimed.
But the core finding holds up well.
When we watch someone else, we routinely underestimate the pressures they're under.
So what do we do with that?
Part three. Writing the other story.
The first habit is the simplest.
When someone does something that annoys you, invent at least one situational explanation before you settle on a character judgement.
It doesn't have to be true.
It just has to be possible.
The American writer David Foster Wallace described this beautifully in a graduation speech he gave at Kenyon College in 2005, which later became known as This Is Water.
To paraphrase him, he talks about being stuck in traffic and angry at the driver of a huge car who has just cut him off.
Then he points out that it's not impossible that the driver is a father rushing a sick or injured child to hospital, and that his hurry is far more urgent than anyone else's.
Wallace wasn't saying that's what was really happening.
He was saying we get to choose which story we tell, and the default one isn't the only option.
The second habit is to ask what would make a reasonable person do this.
A colleague misses a deadline.
Instead of deciding they're lazy, ask what would have to be true for a decent, capable person to miss it.
Maybe they were given conflicting priorities.
Maybe they were never told the date had moved.
Asking this question often turns a complaint into a conversation, and it's the conversation that fixes the problem.
The third habit is to look for patterns rather than moments.
Character is real, and some people really are careless or unkind.
But one incident tells you very little.
A shop assistant who is short with you might be at the end of a ten-hour shift after a customer just abused them.
If you see the same behaviour many times, in many different situations, then it's more reasonable to think it says something about the person.
And the fourth habit is to turn the lens around.
When you catch yourself explaining away your own mistake with your circumstances, pause and ask whether you'd give someone else the same benefit of the doubt.
The aim isn't to be harder on yourself.
It's to be as fair to others as you already are to you.
Let's recap.
The fundamental attribution error is our tendency to explain other people's behaviour by their character while underestimating the situation they're in.
Studies from quizmasters to hurried seminary students show how much circumstances drive what people do.
So before you judge, imagine a situation that could explain it, and wait for a pattern before deciding who someone really is.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. In the Good Samaritan study, what mattered most in whether students stopped to help?
Answer. Whether they were in a hurry.
Question two. In the quizmaster study, who did people rate as more knowledgeable?
Answer. The quizmasters, even though the roles were assigned at random.
Question three. What's the first habit for avoiding the fundamental attribution error?
Answer. Imagine at least one situational explanation before judging someone's character.
That's the end of The Fundamental Attribution Error. Nicely done.
